abstract: We study online coloring, focusing on the competitive ratio. The best previously known results were (1) a lower bound of $\Omega(n / \log^2 n)$ for both deterministic and randomized algorithms by Halld\'{o}rsson and Szegedy (1994), (2) an upper bound of $O(n / \log n)$ for randomized algorithms by Halld\'{o}rsson (1997), and (3) an upper bound of $O(n / \log \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (2025). In this paper, we improve these results as follows: 1. A new lower bound of $\Omega(n / \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms. 2. A new upper bound of $O(n (\log \log n)^2 / \log^2 n)$ for randomized algorithms. 3. A new upper bound of $O(n / (\log \log n)^{2-\varepsilon})$ for deterministic algorithms for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. For randomized algorithms, we nearly close the gap between the lower and upper bounds; the remaining gap is only $O((\log \log n)^2)$. We establish the asymptotic separation between randomized and deterministic online graph coloring. Against an oblivious adversary, a polynomial-time randomized algorithm achieves a competitive ratio asymptotically smaller than any deterministic algorithm can guarantee, even with unlimited computation.
hook: Randomized online graph coloring provably beats every deterministic algorithm.
summary: The paper tightens the competitive ratio for coloring graphs as their vertices arrive one at a time. It proves a deterministic lower bound of n/log n and a randomized upper bound near n(log log n)^2/log^2 n, which together separate the two kinds of algorithm. A gap of (log log n)^2 remains for randomized algorithms, and the randomized advantage holds against an oblivious adversary only.
title: Online Graph Coloring: Competitive Ratios Separating Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms
